newsitem.title: GREECE: Salomon sees softer drachma, stubborn inflation.
newsitem.headline: Salomon sees softer drachma, stubborn inflation.

text.p: Salomon Brothers expects Greece's marker 12-month T-bill rate to fall to 12.0 percent by year-end from 12.7 percent now and to decline only marginally in 1997 as prospects for further inflation easing will be limited.

"The scope for further interest rate cuts will be limited until inflation pressures ease. A more rapid decline in interest rates would require either a significant drop in the public sector borrowing requirement (PSBR) or a postponement of wage increases," it said. "Neither of these is likely to materialise in 1997," Salomon said in a report that focused on Greece's national elections on September 22.

The deterioration in Greece's external balance and the still high inflation differential between Greece and the European Union suggest that a fixed exchange rate policy may be difficult to maintain next year.

"It thus appears likely that irrespective of the outcome of the September election the authorities may let the drachma depreciate by 3-4 percent next year to restore competitiveness," Salomon Brothers economist Miranda Xafa said.
After gaining in the first half of the year, the drachma retracted slightly in July and August in line with authorities' objective to keep it roughly stable on average during the year.

Noting markets reacted positively to the announcement of early elections it said this was expected to alleviate the risk of short term political influence on the 1997 budget which will be submitted to parliament in November.
Greece's fiscal target based on its EU convergence plan was likely to be exceeded this year due to a shortfall in tax revenues and higher than expected interest rates.
"The 1996 general government deficit will probably reach 9.0 percent of GDP compared to a 7.6 percent target," the report said.
"Next year's deficit target of 4.2 percent of GDP appears unattainable irrespective of the election outcome, putting at risk the objective of stabilising the public debt ratio."
Further efforts to restrain expenditure through a tight incomes policy was bound to meet resistance after five years of faling real wages.
The authorities need to seek other means to cut spending including privatisation and closure of unprofitable state- controlled companies and redundant public entities, Salomon said.

"However, neither of the two major parties has campaigned for aggressive privatisation and economic deregulation. Wide-ranging structural reforms are therefore unlikely to be implemented irrespective of the outcome of the national election," it said. --George Georgiopoulos, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
